analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for companies to classify workers as independent contractors under federal wage law.
analysis.headline: Tim Scott's bill to narrow who counts as an "employee" under federal wage-and-hour law never got a vote, dying in the Senate labor committee with 5 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the Fair Labor Standards Act so that the definition of "employee" follows the narrower common-law control test, the same test the IRS uses, instead of the broader standard courts currently use under wage-and-hour law. That would let more companies treat workers as independent contractors. Workers classified that way lose their federal right to minimum wage and overtime pay; companies save the cost of providing them.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that rely on contractor labor — app-based gig platforms, staffing agencies, franchisors, and other employers — would gain if the bill passed. Under the current "suffer or permit to work" standard, courts look at whether a worker is economically dependent on the company; under the common-law test the bill adopts, the question is mainly who controls how the work is done, which is easier for a company to engineer around. Reclassifying workers as contractors frees those companies from minimum wage, overtime, and other Fair Labor Standards Act obligations, and the bill's change to the definition of "employ" would also make it harder to treat a company as a joint employer of someone else's worker.

how_it_helps.text: Rewrites the Fair Labor Standards Act definition of "employee" to follow the usual common-law rules, the same control-focused test used for employment-tax purposes under Internal Revenue Code section 3121(d), replacing the broader standard courts apply under wage-and-hour law.

Changes the definition of "employ" from "suffer or permit to work" to "suffer or permit an employee to work," which narrows whose work a company can be held responsible for and reduces joint-employer exposure for franchisors and companies that rely on subcontractors.

By shrinking the pool of workers counted as employees, the bill would relieve employers of minimum wage, overtime, and other federal wage-and-hour obligations for workers they classify as independent contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who could be reclassified as independent contractors would bear the cost. Someone treated as a contractor loses the federal guarantee of at least the minimum wage for all hours worked, time-and-a-half overtime pay, and the other protections of the Fair Labor Standards Act. The savings show up as lower labor costs for the companies that no longer owe those wages.

drawbacks.text: The bill's core effect is to remove federal wage-and-hour protections from workers companies can structure as contractors: a driver, courier, or home-care aide reclassified under the common-law test would no longer be guaranteed the minimum wage or overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Adopting the IRS common-law test would push wage-and-hour law toward the control-focused analysis used for employment taxes, which is easier for a company to satisfy by dictating results rather than methods — leaving workers with the obligations of a business (no wage floor, no overtime) without the protections of one.

Narrowing the definition of "employ" would also weaken joint-employer liability, making it harder to hold a brand or platform responsible for wage violations committed against workers supplied by its franchisees or subcontractors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers, the bill offers real savings: fewer workers covered by minimum wage and overtime rules, one simpler classification test, and less joint-employer liability. For workers, the cost is direct — anyone shifted to contractor status loses the federal wage floor and overtime guarantee, and gig workers, who often depend heavily on a single app, would be the most exposed. The bill's title frames the change as empowerment, but nothing in the text adds any benefit, bargaining right, or protection to workers; its only operative provisions narrow the definitions that trigger employer obligations. On balance, the value flows to companies that use contractor labor, and the risk falls on the people doing the work.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's labor committee never took the bill up after it was referred there, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Scott introduced the bill on December 4, 2019, together with Senator Marsha Blackburn; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Five Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The HELP Committee took no further action on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept the existing Fair Labor Standards Act standard, which is broader and harder for companies to design around, so the minimum wage and overtime protections the bill would have eroded remain in place. Employers who hoped to reclassify workers as contractors gained nothing, but they also lost nothing they already had.

for.name: Sen. Tim Scott

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Senator Scott on the day it was filed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor, co-introducer, and all five cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, but it never reached a vote so there is no roll-call record of where each party stood.

industries.note: The bill adopts the control-focused common-law test for deciding who is an employee, which makes it easier for platforms to classify drivers and couriers as independent contractors and keeps them outside minimum wage and overtime rules. Workers' gain in flexibility is the platform's saving, but the bill gives workers nothing new in exchange.

A narrower employee definition and a narrower definition of 'employ' reduce the wages these firms must guarantee and the liability they carry for workers they place. The cost of that reduction falls on the placed workers themselves.

By inserting 'an employee' into the definition of 'employ,' the bill would make it harder to hold a franchisor jointly responsible for wage violations at its franchisees, shielding the brand while franchise workers' protections become dependent on their immediate employer's compliance.
